title: Ethanol and its twin
hook: Same nine atoms, same mass, one atom moved. Does the twin boil at the same temperature?

knows: that a liquid boils when its molecules escape into gas
that oxygen pulls electrons harder than hydrogen (bond polarity, who-grabs-the-electrons)
doesNotKnow: that an H on an O (or N, F) lets molecules cling to each other with hydrogen bonds
that this grip between molecules, not their mass, can decide a boiling point

misconception: Molecules made of the same atoms, with the same mass, boil at about the same temperature (boiling point follows weight).
objective: The learner can explain that ethanol boils about 100 °C higher than dimethyl ether, though both are C2H6O, because only ethanol has an H on oxygen to form hydrogen bonds between molecules.

claims.text: Ethanol and dimethyl ether are built from the same nine atoms, C2H6O, with a molar mass of about 46 u (question: 'built from the same nine atoms (C₂H₆O, 46 u)'; reveal: 'Same nine atoms, same 46 u').
claims.source: Structure count (CH3-CH2-OH and CH3-O-CH3: 2 C, 6 H, 1 O each) and IUPAC 2021 standard atomic weights C 12.011, H 1.008, O 15.999: 2(12.011) + 6(1.008) + 15.999 = 46.07 u (node, demo-builder 2026-10-14). Brief claim 1.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Structure count re-done: CH3-CH2-OH and CH3-O-CH3 each have 2 C, 6 H, 1 O = 9 atoms. Node: 2(12.011) + 6(1.008) + 15.999 = 46.069 u (46.068 with the older weights in the chemicals 1.5.2 element table). OpenStax Chemistry 2e section 10.1 (m68761, opened from the openstax GitHub repository) gives 46 g/mol for both, and section 2.4 (m68693) calls them structural isomers of the same composition.

claims.text: At 1 atm ethanol boils at about 78 °C and dimethyl ether at about −24 °C (question; stage record lines 'Ethanol boils 78 °C', 'Dimethyl ether boils −24 °C'; reveal: 'ethanol boils at about 78 °C and dimethyl ether at about −24 °C').
claims.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 'Physical Constants of Organic Compounds': ethanol 78.29 °C, dimethyl ether −24.8 °C (brief claim 2); cross-check PubChem CID 702 and CID 8254. Flag for the fact-checker: −24.8 rounds to −25; the brief and the lesson say 'about −24 °C' (other references list −24 °C). Gap 78.3 − (−24.8) = 103 °C, 'about 100 °C'.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-840, 2026-10-14): reveal no longer says '100 °C apart'; previously unverified. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened data: PyPI chemicals 1.5.2 Tb tables. Ethanol: CRC_ORG 78.24, YAWS 78.29, WEBBOOK 78.35, HEOS 78.42 °C ('about 78 °C'). Dimethyl ether: CRC_ORG -24.8, COMMON_CHEMISTRY -24.8, WEBBOOK -24.15, YAWS -24.84 °C. 'About −24 °C' is within 1 °C of every table (NIST WebBook value -24.15 rounds to -24). Non-blocking: '-25 °C' would match the CRC value more closely.

claims.text: A hydrogen bond needs an H bonded to a strongly electronegative atom (N, O or F) on the donor: the O pulls electrons off its H, leaving it bare (partly positive) to cling to a neighbour's O. Ethanol has one H on its O; dimethyl ether has six H, all on carbon and none on O, so ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other and are held only by weaker attractions (dipole and dispersion), which still make it a liquid below −24 °C (stage legend 'White: H on O', 'Grey: C, each with its own Hs (not drawn)'; reveal: 'With the O in the middle, no H sits on oxygen: 0 dashes, only a weaker pull to break').
claims.source: Arunan et al., 'Definition of the hydrogen bond (IUPAC Recommendations 2011)', Pure Appl. Chem. 83(8), 1637-1641; Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, intermolecular interactions. Structure: CH3-CH2-O-H vs CH3-O-CH3. Brief claim 3.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-840, 2026-10-14): learner r10: 'nothing to break' implied ether molecules have no attraction; now 'only a weaker pull', and the O-H polarity clause added; legend says C atoms carry Hs not drawn; previously unverified. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Opened source: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (git clone openstax/osbooks-chemistry-bundle), module m68761 'Intermolecular Forces': the strong attraction 'may occur when a molecule contains a hydrogen atom bonded to a fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen atom'; the electronegativity difference and small H 'leads to highly concentrated partial charges'; 'Molecules with F-H, O-H, or N-H moieties are very strongly attracted ... hydrogen bonding'; dispersion and dipole-dipole forces are the weaker attractions. Structures: m68693 (ethanol vs methoxymethane/dimethyl ether, same composition) and m68848 ('CH3OCH3: all are tetrahedral'), so all six H of the ether are on carbon. 'Still a liquid below −24 °C' follows from c2. The IUPAC 2011 definition was not opened; it is not needed.

claims.text: Boiling pulls molecules apart, so the grip between them, the hydrogen bond, sets the boiling temperature here, not the weight (reveal).
claims.source: Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, intermolecular interactions and vaporisation; follows from c1-c3 (same mass, different hydrogen bonding, ~100 °C difference). The lesson does not claim hydrogen bonding is the only intermolecular force (dispersion and dipole forces act in both).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Opened OpenStax Chemistry 2e section 10.1 (m68761): same shapes and molar masses (46, 46 g/mol), 'so they will exhibit similar dispersion forces'; ethanol's hydrogen bonding makes the strongest IMFs 'and thus boiling points'. Corroborated by CRC enthalpy of vaporization at Tb (chemicals 1.5.2): ethanol 38.56 kJ/mol vs dimethyl ether 21.51 kJ/mol. The cited Atkins chapter was not opened.

claims.text: The ring of six molecules and its dashes are a schematic of one instant, not a measured count: 6 dashes in the ethanol ring, 2 broken when one molecule is pulled out, 0 for the ether (stage record lines; reveal: 'In your ethanol ring, 6 dashes each linked an O–H to a neighbour's O ... and pulling one out broke 2').
claims.source: The lesson's own drawing (Demo.tsx hBonds(): each ethanol donates one H-bond to its neighbour; pulling molecule 0 breaks the two bonds it takes part in). Cyclic hydrogen-bonded clusters of alcohols exist, but the ring here is illustrative. Brief claim 5. The stage shows only heavy atoms and the H on O; the H atoms on carbon are omitted.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-840, 2026-10-14): reveal wording changed; previously unverified. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Convention: Demo.tsx hBonds() returns 6 bonds for ethanol (each molecule k donates to (k + 1) mod 6), marks the 2 touching molecule 0 broken when it is pulled, and returns [] for the ether. The reveal and record lines say 6, 2 and 0; the stage comment calls the ring schematic of one instant.

recall.question: Two liquids are made of molecules with the same atoms and the same mass. Only one has an H attached to an O. Which one most likely boils at the higher temperature?
options: The one with the H on O
They boil at the same temperature
recall.why: An H on O lets molecules hydrogen-bond to their neighbours. Boiling has to pull them apart, so that grip, not the mass, raises the boiling point.
